taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Texas has important infraspecific complexity; the learner remains species-level while the deep-review draft preserves the M. stanfieldii distinction.
look_here_first: CREW ID: Find an aromatic upright mint with opposite leaves on a square stem and pale white-to-pink leaflike floral bracts under crowded rings of flowers. Look for the ACTUAL cream-to-yellow, often purple-spotted, two-lipped flowers protruding from those tiers. For the critical lemon beebalm comparison, examine the bract tips and the small calyx tube beneath ONE flower with a hand lens: typical spotted horsemint has pointed bracts and shorter, triangular calyx teeth, versus long slender bristles in lemon beebalm. IMPORTANT: Texas M. punctata varieties vary in calyx-tooth length; do not force an ID from one character. In sandy Central Texas habitats also inspect the calyx mouth: M. stanfieldii has a dense whitish hair plug, unlike the generally open/ciliate mouth of M. punctata.

project_inclusion.range_basis: BONAP county distribution cross-check plus regional specimen/field documentation from Travis, Tom Green and Bexar Counties.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Because the M. punctata complex is taxonomically variable in Texas and overlaps with M. stanfieldii, ambiguous garden or seed-mix observations are not used as county-native proof.

best_field_traits: Strongly aromatic annual or short-lived perennial, sometimes persistent depending on variety/site; square or 4-angled often hairy stems
Opposite simple lanceolate to narrow-lanceolate leaves with low, uneven teeth
Flowering axis commonly bears several distinct crowded tiers (verticillasters), with the uppermost tier terminal; stacking alone does NOT split lemon beebalm
Large leaflike white, pale pink, or purplish floral bracts beneath each tier, generally pointed without the long hairlike terminal bristle conspicuous in M. citriodora
Actual tubular two-lipped corollas are cream to pale yellow, often speckled with purple or reddish-brown dots; color and spotting have exceptions
Green ribbed CALYX immediately behind an individual flower ends in five typically short triangular-to-lanceolate teeth, often ciliate; Texas varieties can have longer teeth
Calyx opening is generally open with marginal hairs, not densely sealed by a white-silvery hair plug as in M. stanfieldii
Four dry one-seeded nutlets may develop per flower inside the persistent calyx
morphology_keys.comparison_training: First separate it from M. citriodora by the absence of long bristles on the bracts/calyx teeth. For the critical Central Texas M. stanfieldii comparison, inspect the calyx mouth: open/ciliate in M. punctata versus densely plugged with white/silvery hairs in M. stanfieldii.
crew_20_second_sequence: 1 · FROM A STEP AWAY: Look for multiple separated tiers with big paperlike bracts around each tier. Compare the whole flowering stem; not the color alone.
2 · CHECK THE LEAVES AND STEM: Opposite narrow leaves, square somewhat hairy stem and aromatic mint smell establish Lamiaceae but not the species.
3 · FIND ONE ACTUAL FLOWER: Cream/yellowish corolla with visible purple/red spotting is good support. This is the curved tubular petal structure, not the pale leafy bract.
4 · IDENTIFY THE CALYX: Follow the corolla back to its small green, ribbed tube; inspect the five tooth tips with a hand lens. Don't point at large floral bracts and call them calyx teeth.

5 · RULE OUT THE CLOSEST LOOK-ALIKES: M. citriodora often has conspicuously BRISTLE-TIPPED bracts and calyx teeth, while M. stanfieldii has a SILVERY HAIR PLUG closing the calyx mouth. Varietal overlap means a specimen may require closer review.
morphology_keys.habit: Annual, short-lived perennial or occasionally perennial in the species complex, typically 30–120 cm, erect and often branching; texture and stature vary by variety and site. Do not rely on longevity for species ID.
morphology_keys.stems_and_leaves: Stems square/4-angled, hairy, aromatic. Leaves opposite, simple, usually lanceolate or narrowly oblong, often approximately 2–9 cm long and up to 2.5 cm wide in the 2023 detailed species account; margins show shallow teeth, sometimes reduced on upper leaves. Mint-family leaf characters are shared with other Monarda.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Several (often 1–4 or sometimes more) dense false whorls (verticillasters), separated by internodes, with showy leaflike upper bracts reaching around or below each tier. A single head on a small shoot does not rule out this species.
morphology_keys.floral_bracts: A bract is a LEAFLIKE STRUCTURE beneath the cluster, NOT the flower's petals and NOT the calyx tube surrounding a single flower. M. punctata bracts are commonly whitish, pink or lavender with acute/acuminate tips; their color and outline overlap M. citriodora and seasonal conditions.
morphology_keys.corolla: One actual flower has a distinctly bilabiate (two-lipped) narrow tubular corolla, typically cream/pale yellow with many purple spots; the arching hairy upper lip curves like a hood, and the lower lip broadens and divides into three lobes. Unspotted or lightly marked forms occur; repeated observations outperform one flower.
morphology_keys.calyx: The CALYX is the smaller green, ribbed tube of fused sepals behind ONE flower. Five lobes/teeth surround its opening; typical M. punctata teeth are short, triangular or triangular-lanceolate. UT Austin's Williamson County var. intermedia treatment specifically measures the teeth about 0.5–1 mm and describes them as not stiff-pointed. Other varieties vary in calyx pubescence and tooth shape, so compare multiple structures instead of treating tooth length alone as an absolute species diagnostic.
morphology_keys.stanfieldii_tie_breaker: M. stanfieldii is a locally important Texas species historically confused with M. punctata. M. stanfieldii has a calyx mouth plugged with an unusually dense whitish/silvery hair mass and a relatively hairless corolla tube; typical M. punctata has an open but ciliate calyx mouth. Check a spent flower with a lens; do not make an identification from a distant pale head.
morphology_keys.fruit: The ovary commonly yields up to four distinct smooth, dry, one-seeded nutlets per single flower, hidden in the persistent calyx. An entire spent tier is NOT a four-nutlet fruit macro; the actual units require dissection/magnification. Go Botany documents mericarps approximately 1.3–1.5 mm.
morphology_keys.central_texas_field_context: Open sunny sandy to rocky ground, roadsides, native plant beds, prairie edges, and disturbed soils. In Texas commonly flowers spring through summer, sometimes later after favorable rains. The 2023 photographed Abair examples used for the diagnostic close-ups are from Florida and document species structures, not local Hays provenance.
morphology_keys.crew_management: In routine landscape visits, a pale showy whorl is not automatically an exotic or something needing removal. Observe opposite leaves and true corollas before deciding. Leave flowering and seed-bearing stems where the design and safety constraints allow. The species supplies nectar/pollen and NPSOT lists larval associations, but do not invent local host-species or specialty-bee counts.

botanical_vocabulary.Corolla: The actual two-lipped petals on an individual flower. In punctata, typically cream-yellow with purple spotting.
botanical_vocabulary.Calyx: The smaller green tube directly behind one corolla, ending in five teeth; hairy mouth is examined with a hand lens.
botanical_vocabulary.Floral bract: The broad white/pink/purple leaflike modified leaves under an entire tier, usually larger than one calyx.
botanical_vocabulary.Verticillaster: A densely clustered false whorl of many individual flowers; repeated tiers along a stem.
botanical_vocabulary.Ciliate: Fringed with small hairs along a margin. An OPEN hairy calyx mouth is different from a closed white hair plug.
botanical_vocabulary.Nutlet: A tiny one-seeded dry fruit unit; up to four from one flower.

comparisons.key_distinctions: M. citriodora has long bristle-tipped floral bracts and calyx teeth. M. stanfieldii has a dense white/silvery hair plug closing the calyx mouth. M. fistulosa lacks the characteristic cream/yellow heavily spotted corollas and tiered pale bracts.

field_matrix.flower_corolla: Usually cream/yellow, strongly purple-spotted; unspotted variants known
field_matrix.bract_tip: Broad pale/pink bract, usually acute or acuminate without an obvious several-mm threadlike awn
field_matrix.calyx: Generally shorter triangular/lanceolate teeth, mouth typically OPEN with fringe; geographic varieties vary
field_matrix.flowering_stem: Can have stacked separated tiers; length and abundance vary
field_matrix.best_crew_check: See the individual spotted flower, then check calyx mouth and bract tip; not spots alone.

field_matrix.flower_corolla: Usually white, pink or lavender, sometimes also spotted/marked
field_matrix.bract_tip: Bracts more commonly with long thin spine/bristle at apex (2–5 mm reported)
field_matrix.calyx: Longer slender bristle-like teeth, often 2–7 mm in Texas regional floras
field_matrix.flowering_stem: ALSO tiered; pale flower forms exist
field_matrix.best_crew_check: Close-up actual BRISTLE on bract and CALYX, not just purplish color.

field_matrix.flower_corolla: Similar to spotted horsemint, colors overlap
field_matrix.calyx: Mouth becomes plugged CLOSED by dense white-silver hairs (versus open but ciliate)
field_matrix.best_crew_check: Close-up spent calyx mouth under a hand lens; critical central Texas comparison.

field_matrix.bract_tip: Lacks repeated showy pale/purple floral rings typical of punctata
field_matrix.calyx: Different and variable; verify if needed
field_matrix.flowering_stem: Usually a single broader rounded terminal head rather than several stacked tiers
field_matrix.best_crew_check: Compare entire flowering stem silhouette, then floral structures; not one close flower.

do_not_trust_alone: Bract color: pink/white occurs in both punctata and citriodora.
Purple spots: characteristic but not universal in punctata, and corolla markings can occur in citriodora.
Several stacked rings: shared by punctata and citriodora.
A bract apex called a calyx tooth: they are anatomically different and must be labeled separately.
Short calyx teeth for EVERY punctata: Texas infraspecific variants include relatively elongate teeth.
Open calyx throat from an out-of-focus image: M. stanfieldii requires a properly focused close look.

visual_comparison.title: Spotted horsemint — point to the COROLLA, BRACT, and CALYX

visual_comparison.memory_rule: PALE BRACT ≠ PALE FLOWER. Find the cream/spotted two-lipped corolla, then trace its SMALL green calyx. Lemon beebalm often adds conspicuous bristle tips; Stanfield's beebalm closes the calyx throat with a silvery plug.

items.caption: Trace two flower tiers on one green-brown stem. The broad hanging PURPLE-PINK structures are bracts, not petals; the pale curved, purple-spotted structures above each tier are actual corollas. Labels refer only to visible features in the original photo.
items.why_it_matters: Both Monarda species can have tiers, but the punctuation-like purple spots are a strong support clue when combined with bract and calyx structure.

items.label: 3 — Actual corolla: purple spots, upper and lower lip
items.image_role: Macro front view of one white-to-cream spotted two-lipped corolla with green bracts behind

items.caption: In the image, follow the white/lilac speckled curving petals backward to the green RIBBED tube below: that green tube is a calyx. field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Spotted horsemint: inspect these three details first
steps: First find ONE real cream-to-yellow tubular flower, often purple-spotted, protruding from the stacked tiers. The broad pale/pink modified leaves are bracts, NOT corolla petals.
Check the BRACt tip: ordinarily pointed without the long, abruptly narrowing bristle that lemon beebalm often has. Colors vary in both species.

Trace the real flower to its small ribbed calyx tube. Typical spotted horsemint has shorter triangular teeth; Texas varieties vary. If you have a sandy-country suspected Monarda stanfieldii, look for a plugged white/silver hairy calyx mouth (punctata is generally open/ciliate).
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: These arrows are positioned over actual photographed structures; please inspect the zoomable original to confirm a difficult character. Not every photo shows a calyx tooth or bract tip clearly. If you can't see the structure, stop at Monarda sp. until a close-up or specimen is available.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: The fine calyx and bract differences are tendencies across regional varieties, not absolute for every photograph. Do not use color or tier count alone.
